title: Supreme Court to Hear Arguments Wednesday on State Bans on AR-15 Rifles
excerpt: Challenges to Connecticut's and Cook County's assault-style weapon bans reach the 6-3 conservative court, in a case that turns on whether America's most popular rifle is in 'common use' — and therefore cannot be banned.
body:
• The Supreme Court hears arguments on Wednesday, December 2, over state and local bans on AR-15-style rifles — challenges to Connecticut's ban and Cook County, Illinois's ordinance, in one of the most significant Second Amendment cases in decades.
  • Challengers argue the AR-15 is in "common use" — their main brief uses the phrase 56 times, and the Trump administration's supporting brief 49 times — and that arms in common use cannot be banned under the court's 2008 Heller precedent.
  • Connecticut and Cook County argue governments have restricted unusually dangerous weapons since medieval England, and that the AR-15's military lineage and design place it outside constitutional protection.
  • A decision is expected in the spring. Eleven states and the District of Columbia ban assault-style weapons, according to Everytown for Gun Safety.

Fourteen years after a lone gunman carried out the deadliest elementary school shooting in American history, the Supreme Court is turning to a bitter legal fight over whether communities may outlaw the type of weapon used in that massacre — a popular class of semi-automatic guns that includes the AR-15. The justices will hear arguments on Wednesday, December 2, over state and local bans on "assault-style" weapons, some enacted or strengthened after 20 first graders and six educators were killed in 2012 at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut, CNN reports.

The two cases

The case before the court is known as Viramontes v. Cook County, but it combines two lawsuits: one challenging Cook County's ban and another challenging Connecticut's. Cook County residents Cutberto Viramontes and Christopher Khaya, members of the Firearms Policy Coalition, first sued over the county's ban in 2021. On October 29, Viramontes asked the Supreme Court to drop him from the case without providing a reason; the court granted the request on November 23, but Khaya and other challengers remain, and the Connecticut case — granted in June — would continue even if the Cook County litigation were dismissed, according to the North Dakota Monitor's report. The court focused the question it will answer on the AR-15 and "similar semiautomatic rifles." Lower federal appeals courts — the 7th Circuit in the Cook County case and the 2nd Circuit in the Connecticut dispute — upheld both bans.

The challengers' argument: common use

Gun rights groups focus first on the weapon's popularity. As many as 26 million Americans own an AR-15 or similar rifle by one survey estimate; a 2022 Washington Post-Ipsos survey works out to about 16 million. The Supreme Court acknowledged last year, in a unanimous opinion, that the weapons are "widely legal," purchased by "many ordinary consumers," and that the AR-15 "is the most popular rifle in the country." The plaintiffs described the AR-15 as the "paradigmatic American rifle" and told the justices that Justice Antonin Scalia's 2008 precedent in District of Columbia v. Heller "stands for the proposition that arms in common use cannot be banned." They reject the claim that an AR-15 is more dangerous than other guns, noting its most common caliber is smaller than that of many traditional hunting rifles: "These are ordinary rifles," they wrote, "not phasers from Star Trek."

"This is one of the most important Second Amendment cases in American history. The question is simple: Can the government ban some of the most popular firearms in America?"

— Brandon Combs, President, Firearms Policy Coalition

The defence: dangerous and unusual

Connecticut and Cook County lean on the court's 2022 precedent, New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, which held that modern gun regulations need grounding in the "nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation." The state and county say there is an extensive history — dating to medieval times — of English laws banning especially dangerous weapons. "From fourteenth-century England to twenty-first century America, governments have restricted weapons because of their unusually dangerous properties," Connecticut officials told the court. They also note the AR-15's ties to its military counterpart, the M16. Cook County State's Attorney Eileen O'Neill Burke, who is defending her county's ban, said: "The basic function of government is to keep its citizenry safe, and these guns are so incredibly dangerous in a densely populated area like Chicago. It was designed for the military. It was designed to take out enemy combatants at the greatest distance possible."

Counting to five

At least four conservative justices have signaled skepticism of the bans to varying degrees. Justice Clarence Thomas wrote in 2015 that lower courts upholding the bans were "relegating the Second Amendment to a second-class right," and Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in the Maryland AR-15 case that, given millions of owners, challengers had a "strong argument" that AR-15s are protected. That leaves Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Amy Coney Barrett as the justices to watch on Wednesday. Billy Clark, associate litigation director at the Giffords Law Center, which supports the bans, said Roberts and Barrett "have articulated a history-based test that looks for something useful in the history," and that Roberts "recognizes the consequences" of the court's decisions. After arguments, the justices will likely release a decision in the spring — one that will decide the fate of bans in the 11 states and the District of Columbia that have them, and could stop Congress from imposing new prohibitions on some semiautomatic weapons.
